Soil-erosion risk, a ranked work list with reasons, and season-by-season monitoring for the whole of Assam. Built on the same data backbone that already runs two live hazard forecasts in Arunachal Pradesh.

What if we treat it?

Monitoring: bare ground every dry season, 2019–2026

In the hills, jhum plots are cleared in winter and burned in March–April; the ground stays bare until the crop grows after the monsoon starts. The monsoon's heavy rain falls on whatever the dry season left bare, so that is the season SoilSense measures: every 100 m square, from Sentinel-2's 10 m pictures, 1 February – 30 April, every year.

Land seen clearly each season: 2019 100%, 2020 100%, 2021 100%, 2022 100%, 2023 100%, 2024 100%, 2025 100%, 2026 100%. Squares too cloudy are left blank, never guessed.

Each year's bare ground also re-runs the recipe ("loss with this year's cover"), and the catchments that got barer are listed. Flags for new bare ground on a steep slope are held back until they pass the tests on the Checks page; the measured bare ground is shown meanwhile.

Two errors caught before any result existed

1 · The usual rain formula reads 91% low in Assam

Most Indian erosion studies turn annual rainfall into rain strength with one formula. At Guwahati, the only place with a published measured value, it gives a tenth of the real figure. We use the satellite-based InRESatE map (−5%), keep IRED alongside, and tested both against 40 rain gauges.

2 · The national 250 m map barely responds to slope

Our slope factor rises 500-fold from flat land to steep hills; the national map's rises about twofold. That is why the national map rates western Assam's plains among India's most erodible, while ours puts the hills (Dima Hasao, the Karbi hills, the hills of south Kamrup and Cachar) first.

How it is built

  • The data backbone is the core. Each source is fetched by a script and stored untouched, with its source, licence, link, date and checksum. Every layer is fitted to one 100 m grid. A region switch moved it from Arunachal Pradesh to Assam in about four weeks; the live Arunachal forecasts are re-checked after every change to shared code.
  • The recipe is transparent. RUSLE, the standard used in Indian soil conservation, with each factor kept as its own layer, so an officer can see why a place ranks high.
  • AI beside the formula, never instead of it. Under development: a gradient-boosted model learned from ISRO's mapped eroded land, tested on areas it never saw, with the reasons for each score. Planned: a panel of different models (formula, tree models, deep learning) blended by a referee model, learned across the Himalaya and North East and fine-tuned for Assam and each district; satellite-reading AI for forest, tea, jhum and fresh clearing.
  • Outputs open anywhere: GeoTIFF, GeoPackage, KML, GeoJSON, CSV, in WGS84 or UTM 46N; a web app that needs no installation.

Proof that the backbone works: two live products in Arunachal Pradesh

SoilSense is the third product on the same backbone and the first in a second state. The same team, the same pipeline, the same way of testing.

What comes next

Everything SoilSense will provide

Every item carries one of two labels, the same as in our application answers. Under development: built and working in the app on real Assam data, still being improved and tested. Planned: on our plan, for the programme (phases on the plan page) or after it. Features that fail their tests are held back until they pass.

Under development

  • Erosion-risk map, all Assam, 100 m (RUSLE), with land not assessed marked
  • Priority list of catchments and districts: cause, typical measures, rank firmness, re-ranking
  • AI erosion map trained on ISRO's eroded land, as a second opinion with its reasons
  • Dry-season bare and burnt ground every year since 2019 (Sentinel-2)
  • Weekly erosive-rain outlook from the live forecast, graded against past monsoons
  • Soil reaching streams; value of soil lost (nutrients as urea bags and rupees, topsoil depth)
  • "What if we treat it?": soil saved by each measure
  • Village card for any place; field kit with GPS visit points and GIS downloads

Planned

  • AI panel: formula, tree and deep-learning models blended by a referee model; learned across the Himalaya and North East, fine-tuned for Assam and each district, local-only models kept alongside; retrained after every monsoon
  • Satellite-reading AI for forest, tea, jhum and fresh clearing, with jhum burn dating; radar monitoring through monsoon cloud
  • Alerts for newly cleared slopes and hill cutting, sent only after an AI second check
  • Seasonal outlook and a pre-monsoon watch list for divisions each April
  • "Did the works help?" tracking; a works planner with costs; outputs shaped for PMKSY watershed and MGNREGA plans
  • Stream sensors, rain gauges and soil-loss plots where the model points; drone and LiDAR surveys
  • Offline field app in Assamese; farmers' photo reports sorted by AI and checked by a person; SMS, WhatsApp and voice advisories; an AI assistant for officers
  • Riverbank erosion, flood sand on farmland, wetland and reservoir silting; landslide and flood forecasts for Assam on the same platform

Pilot, to agree with the department

Dima Hasao and the Karbi hills (steep, jhum, erosion a known concern), plus one foothill belt for contrast. A field protocol dated before any visit: blind points stratified across classes and top-ranked catchments; teams record rills, gullies, bare soil, sediment and existing works without seeing the map's class; agreement measured against a pass mark set in advance.

Data

Built on open data: Copernicus DEM GLO-30, SoilGrids (CC-BY), ESA WorldCover (CC-BY), Sentinel-2 via Google Earth Engine, InRESatE and IRED rain-strength maps (CC-BY), HydroSHEDS, Survey of India outline, NASA GPM IMERG and Open-Meteo rain, CWC river-sediment and river-level records. Used for comparison only, never redistributed: the IIT Delhi national erosion map (IWED), India's soil-erodibility map (ISED). NRSC's land-degradation map (Bhuvan): training labels for the AI map and an outside check, never redistributed. Ours: the backbone code, region switch, ranking and reasons, change detection, AI model and training pipeline, checks, app and the checked local record.
